title: Princess Tarakanova
source: State Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow (public domain). Wikimedia Commons: 1862 Flavitsky Prinzessin Tarakanow anagoria.JPG (3367 x 4897 px). The '1862' in the file name is wrong for this canvas: the Tretyakov version is dated 1864; a presumed earlier version (1862) is in Ekaterinburg.
caption: She claimed to be the daughter of an empress. Nobody knows her real name, and this painting tells a story that never happened. #russianhistory #catherinethegreat #flavitsky #masterpiece #artfacts
_verify: VERIFIED, Wikipedia EN (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Tarakanova_(painting)): Flavitsky, 1864, oil on canvas, 245 x 187 cm, State Tretyakov Gallery; first shown at the Academy of Arts exhibition in 1864; a casemate of the Peter and Paul Fortress, water flowing through a barred window, a young woman standing on a bed, wet rats crawling out of the water toward her feet; based on the legend that she died in the flood of 21 September 1777; actually died of consumption (tuberculosis) on 4 December 1775, without revealing the secret of her birth even to a priest; Ekaterinburg holds a presumed original of 1862, so the Commons file name's '1862' does not match the Tretyakov canvas (1864).

VERIFIED, Nineteenth-Century Art Worldwide, Chukcheeva, Spring 2023 (19thc-artworldwide.org/spring23/chukcheeva-on-konstantin-flavitsky-princess-tarakanova-of-1864): centrepiece of the 1864-65 Academy exhibition, a succès de scandale that drew bigger crowds than earlier exhibitions; critic Mikhail Dmitriev found it repulsive, a form of 'moral torture'; Tretyakov bought it after Flavitsky's death in 1866 for 4,000 silver rubles; flood story 'entirely legendary'; she died 4 (15) December 1775, apparently of tuberculosis. The article notes the animals look like large mice, though usually called rats; slides say rats (as Wikipedia).

VERIFIED, National Geographic (nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/catherine-the-great-russia-imposter-heir) and Wikipedia EN (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Tarakanova): she claimed to be the daughter of Empress Elizabeth (and Razumovsky); real name and birthplace unknown; aliases included Princess Vladimirskaya, Fräulein Frank, Madame Trémouille; Catherine II sent Count Alexei Orlov, who courted her and proposed marriage in Livorno, lured her aboard a Russian ship and had her seized (February 1775); held in the Peter and Paul Fortress, interrogated by Prince Golitsyn; the name 'Tarakanova' was given later, not used in her lifetime.
CAUTIOUS, slide 4 says Orlov 'courted her in Italy': NatGeo says he feigned passion and proposed, Wikipedia says he seduced her. 'Italy' = Livorno.
UNVERIFIED, not used: the later legend that she survived as the nun Dosifea in Moscow (Wikipedia mentions it as popular belief). Good for a comment reply only, flagged as legend.
Focus boxes estimated from the contact sheet thumbnail; re-tune on the real image (rats on the bed and at the bed corner, slide 6, are the least certain).

slides.headline: Who was the woman in red?
A flooding cell
slides.text: A prison cell in St Petersburg's Peter and Paul Fortress. Water bursts through the barred window, and a young woman climbs onto her bed.

slides.headline: An empress's daughter?
slides.text: She claimed to be the secret daughter of Empress Elizabeth, rightful heir to Russia's throne. Her real name? Still unknown today.

slides.headline: A threat to Catherine
slides.text: Catherine the Great saw a rival. So in 1775 Count Alexei Orlov courted her in Italy, then lured her aboard a Russian ship.

slides.headline: Water at the window
slides.text: She was seized and locked up here. And legend says that when the great flood of 1777 poured in, she drowned.

slides.headline: Rats on the bed
slides.text: Look closer at the bed: wet rats climb out of the water toward her feet. One critic called the picture 'moral torture'. Crowds flocked anyway.

slides.headline: The flood never came
slides.text: But here's the twist: the water never reached her. She had died two years earlier, in December 1775, of tuberculosis.

slides.headline: A legend wins
slides.text: Flavitsky painted the legend anyway, and it stuck. Even the name Tarakanova was given later. She never used it.

slides.headline: Her secret
slides.text: She died without revealing her origins, not even to a priest. Clever impostor or real lost princess: what do you think?
